explanations.explanation: Lies is right, friend. The LORD says, "Ephraim surrounds Me with lies…" and then adds that the house of Israel does it with deceit. That's a whole crowd of falsehood closing in. Ephraim is the northern kingdom of Israel, and the charge starts right here.

Praise would be a nice crowd to be surrounded by, like a surprise party where everybody actually shows up. But that's not what the text says. The LORD says Ephraim surrounds Him with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit. The word is lies, and it's where the charge begins.

Gifts sound lovely, friend, but nobody is handing the LORD a present here. He says Ephraim surrounds Him with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit. Ephraim is the northern kingdom of Israel. Nothing in this line is wrapped up with a bow.

True! The text says, "but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One." Judah is the southern kingdom, and after all that talk of lies, this one little word "but" lands like a cool breeze in a hot kitchen. Still walking, still faithful. That's what the LORD says about Judah in this line.

Not quite, baker. The text says the opposite: "but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One." Judah is the southern kingdom. After the lies of Ephraim, that "but" turns the line toward Judah, and it says Judah is still walking with God.
Olive oil, yes! Ephraim "…makes a covenant with Assyria and sends olive oil to Egypt." Assyria gets the covenant, and Egypt gets the olive oil. Ephraim has his hands in both places.

Fine linen sounds fancy, friend, but it's not in the text. The line says Ephraim "…makes a covenant with Assyria and sends olive oil to Egypt." That's olive oil, plain and simple. Assyria was a powerful empire, and Ephraim is dealing with both it and Egypt.

Silver is a good guess, since it's what people reach for when they want to impress somebody. But the text doesn't say it. Ephraim "…makes a covenant with Assyria and sends olive oil to Egypt." So the shipment going to Egypt is olive oil.

Careful with that "no matter what," friend. The text says, "He will punish Jacob according to his ways and repay him according to his deeds." That's according to his ways and deeds, so the punishment is tied to what Jacob's line has actually done. The answer is False.

False is right. The text says, "He will punish Jacob according to his ways and repay him according to his deeds." The word is according, so it's tied to ways and deeds. The punishment follows what has been done.
Heel is it! "In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel…" The man was holding on before he'd even been introduced to anybody. I've got a mustache for hands, and I still wouldn't try that.
Hand makes sense, friend. That's usually what we grab with. But the text says, "In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel…" The word is heel.

Arm is a fair guess, friend, since a grab like that sounds like an arm job. But the text is more specific: "In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel…" Down at the bottom, the heel. Nobody's guessing arm after that one.

explanations.answer: He weeps and seeks His favor
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says "he wept and sought His favor…" So the story doesn't stop at the win. The wrestler is crying and asking for favor, and the text also says he found Him at Bethel.

explanations.answer: He walks off without a word
explanations.explanation: No silent walk-off here, friend. The text says Jacob "…wept and sought His favor…" and that "he found Him at Bethel and spoke with Him there…" Walking off isn't what the text shows.

explanations.answer: He laughs and boasts of his win
explanations.explanation: You'd expect a victory lap, friend, and I'd probably take two. But the text says Jacob "…wept and sought His favor…" Tears, not a boast. He struggled with the angel and prevailed, and he also wept and sought His favor.

Yes! "But you must return to your God…" After Jacob's story comes that "But," and the prophecy turns. It's a call to come back to God, plain and direct. And I think it lands softer than it sounds, since Jacob wept and sought favor and found Him.
Bethel is in the story, since Jacob found Him there. But the call doesn't send anybody to a town. It says, "But you must return to your God…" The return is to God Himself.
No construction crew needed, friend. The call is, "But you must return to your God…" Nothing in this line asks anyone to build an altar. It's about coming back to God Himself.

Always is right. The call says "maintain love and justice, and always wait on your God." Always, not just when it's easy. I set a timer and hover over my oven like it owes me money, so waiting is not my best skill. That's why I like that word.
Rarely would make waiting very easy, friend, but it's not what the text says. The call is to "maintain love and justice, and always wait on your God." The word is always.
Sometimes is tempting, since we all like a flexible schedule. But the text says, "maintain love and justice, and always wait on your God." It's always, and it comes right alongside love and justice.

True. Ephraim says, "How rich I have become! I have found wealth for myself." Notice it's all I and myself. That's a man admiring his own wallet, and I've caught myself admiring a perfect batch the same way.
Actually, he does, baker. The text has Ephraim boasting, "How rich I have become! I have found wealth for myself." That's right there in the line. The statement is True.

explanations.answer: No one can find sinful iniquity in him
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Ephraim says, "In all my labors, they can find in me no iniquity that is sinful." He's claiming a spotless record. And the very next words from the LORD begin with "But," so the claim doesn't get the last word.

explanations.answer: He has worked harder than his brothers
explanations.explanation: That sounds like something a guy would say at a family dinner, friend. But the text doesn't have Ephraim saying it. His claim is, "In all my labors, they can find in me no iniquity that is sinful." It's about having no sinful iniquity, not about beating his brothers.

explanations.answer: He has given all his wealth away
explanations.explanation: Giving it all away isn't what Ephraim says, friend. He says, "How rich I have become! I have found wealth for myself." Then he claims, "In all my labors, they can find in me no iniquity that is sinful." His claim is about having no sinful iniquity.

Tents! The LORD says, "I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast." Notice the word again. It says dwelling in tents has happened before, and the LORD ties it to the days of the appointed feast.
Palaces would be a big upgrade, friend, but the text goes the other way. The LORD says, "I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast." The word is tents, not palaces.

Cities are a fair guess, friend, since that's where most folks settle down. But the text says, "I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast." The answer is tents. Nobody's calling a realtor for this one.

Not through the kings, baker. The LORD says, "I spoke through the prophets and multiplied their visions; I gave parables through the prophets." He names the prophets, and says it twice. So the answer is False.

False is right. The LORD says, "I spoke through the prophets and multiplied their visions; I gave parables through the prophets." Twice in one verse He says through the prophets. When something's said twice that clearly, it's worth remembering.

explanations.answer: Heaps of stones in the field
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the one. The text says, "…their altars will be heaps of stones in the furrows of the field." The question is about sacrificing bulls in Gilgal, a town in Israel, and it's the altars that become those heaps. Those altars won't stay standing.
Gold is a shiny guess, friend, but the text goes the opposite direction. It says, "…their altars will be heaps of stones in the furrows of the field." Heaps of stones, sitting in a field.

Lasting forever would be a big promise, and the text doesn't make it. It says, "…their altars will be heaps of stones in the furrows of the field." Heaps of stones in a field, friend. That's the opposite of a pillar, and nobody's putting a plaque on a pile.

A wife, yes! The text says, "…Israel worked for a wife—for a wife he tended sheep." Same man as Jacob, since Genesis 32:28 says his name was changed to Israel. Sheep for a wife, friend. That's quite a story.

A house! Friend, after my years stuck in the back of a junk drawer, a roof sounds mighty good to me too. But the text says, "…Israel worked for a wife—for a wife he tended sheep." He wasn't out there with the flock for a roof. He was out there for her.
A field makes sense for a shepherd, friend, but it's not what the text says. It says, "…Israel worked for a wife—for a wife he tended sheep." That's the reason he was out with the sheep.

A prophet, yes! "But by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved." The LORD is the one doing the bringing out, and He does it by a prophet. The same line says that by a prophet Israel was preserved.

A king is a natural guess, friend, since kings usually get the credit. But the text says, "But by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved." So the answer is a prophet.

An army sounds like a big, loud way to do it, but that's not what the text says. It says, "But by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved." The LORD did it by a prophet.

That's right, and I think this one is heavy. The text says, "…his Lord will leave his bloodguilt upon him…" The line comes after Ephraim has provoked bitter anger. It goes on to say his Lord will repay him for his contempt.
Riches fit with the boasting from earlier, friend, but they're not what the text says. It says, "…his Lord will leave his bloodguilt upon him…" This line is serious, and the answer is his bloodguilt.

A blessing would be a gentle ending, but this line doesn't end gently. The text says, "…his Lord will leave his bloodguilt upon him…" It follows the words that Ephraim has provoked bitter anger. The answer is his bloodguilt.
